name: Yuwen Kai
bio: Sui dynasty engineer and city planner who laid out the new capital Daxing, later Tang Chang'an, the largest planned city of its age.
bio_full: Yuwen Kai came from an aristocratic family of Xianbei descent that had served the Northern Zhou, and entered the service of the new Sui dynasty when it reunified China in 581. The following year Emperor Wen commissioned him to plan a new capital south-east of the old Han city of Chang'an. The result, Daxing, was a vast walled rectangle of about 84 square kilometres. Under Emperor Yang he went on to plan the eastern capital at Luoyang, worked on canals, and produced designs for imperial ritual buildings and portable palaces.

Yuwen Kai's Daxing was a grid of 108 walled wards around broad avenues, with the palace and government city at the north and markets to east and west. Renamed Chang'an by the Tang, it became the cosmopolitan metropolis of the Silk Road and the model for capitals across East Asia, including Heijō-kyō (Nara) and Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in Japan. None of his buildings survives above ground, but excavations have confirmed the regularity of his plan.

name: Li Chun
bio: Sui dynasty stonemason credited with the Anji (Zhaozhou) Bridge, the world's oldest surviving open-spandrel segmental stone arch bridge.
bio_full: Almost nothing is known of Li Chun's life. His name survives through a Tang dynasty inscription recording that the great stone bridge over the Xiao River at Zhaozhou, in present-day Hebei, was the work of the craftsman Li Chun under the Sui. The bridge is usually dated to about 595–605.

The bridge he built was remarkably advanced. Instead of a semicircular arch it uses a flat segmental arch of about 37 metres, and four small arches pierce the spandrels, saving stone, lightening the load on the foundations and letting floodwater pass. Comparable designs did not appear in Europe for many centuries. Li Chun is honoured in China as one of the great engineers of antiquity.

name: Li Jie
bio: Song dynasty official of the Directorate of Buildings who compiled the Yingzao Fashi, the most important pre-modern Chinese treatise on architecture.
bio_full: Li Jie, courtesy name Mingzhong, came from Guancheng in present-day Henan and served for many years in the Directorate of Buildings and Construction at the Northern Song capital Kaifeng, supervising work on palaces, government offices and temples. Around 1097 he was ordered to revise an earlier, unsatisfactory building code. He interviewed carpenters and craftsmen, gathered practice from the workshops and completed the new text in 1100; it was printed by imperial order in 1103.

The Yingzao Fashi ('Treatise on Architectural Methods') set out a modular system based on the cross-section of a standard timber, the cai, from which the sizes of columns, beams and bracket sets were derived in eight grades. It also covered masonry, carpentry, painting and tiling, with labour and material quotas and illustrations. Rediscovered in the twentieth century, it became the key with which Liang Sicheng and his colleagues learned to read surviving Chinese buildings.

name: Kuai Xiang
bio: Ming dynasty master carpenter from Suzhou who is credited with the design of the Forbidden City's main halls and the Tiananmen gate.
bio_full: Kuai Xiang came from a family of carpenters at Xiangshan near Suzhou, a district famous for its building craftsmen. When the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing he was among the craftsmen summoned to build the new palace, completed in 1420. He worked on the palace through several reigns, rebuilding halls after fires, and on tombs and other imperial works, rising from craftsman to a vice minister of works, an extraordinary career for an artisan.

Kuai Xiang is traditionally credited with the design of the Chengtian Gate, the predecessor of today's Tiananmen, and of the three great halls of the Forbidden City, though the palace was the work of a whole bureaucracy of designers and thousands of workers, and the extent of his role is hard to establish. Later sources praised his skill at drawing and his ability to estimate exactly the timber a building would need. He became the patron figure of the Xiangshan builders.

name: Lei family (Yangshi Lei)
bio: Family of designers who ran the Qing court's design office for some two hundred years, producing plans and models for palaces, gardens and imperial tombs.
bio_full: The family's founder, Lei Fada (1619–1693), was a carpenter from Jiangxi who came to Beijing and worked on the rebuilding of palace halls under the Kangxi Emperor. His descendants held the post of head of the imperial design office, the yangshi fang, for seven or eight generations until the end of the Qing, which is why they were known as 'Pattern Lei'. They worked on the Old Summer Palace, the Summer Palace, Chengde and the Eastern and Western Qing Tombs, among many other projects.

The Lei produced drawings and finely made architectural models (tangyang) of pasteboard that were shown to the emperor for approval, showing rooms, furniture and gardens at scale. Thousands of their drawings and models survive in the National Library of China, the Palace Museum and other collections, and were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007. They are the best documentation of how Qing imperial architecture was designed.

name: Ji Cheng
bio: Late Ming garden designer and author of the Yuanye ('The Craft of Gardens'), the only classical Chinese treatise devoted entirely to garden making.
bio_full: Ji Cheng was born in Wujiang near Suzhou and trained as a painter, admiring the landscapes of Jing Hao and Guan Tong. After travelling in his youth he settled in Zhenjiang and began making artificial rockeries, then whole gardens for officials in Changzhou and Yangzhou, including the Garden of Reflections (Yingyuan) of Zheng Yuanxun. His treatise Yuanye, with a preface of 1631, was printed in 1634 with the backing of the politician Ruan Dacheng, whose later disgrace may explain why the book was little read in China for three centuries.

The Yuanye covers siting, buildings, walls, windows, paving, rockeries and the 'borrowing' of views from the surrounding landscape, illustrated with lattice and window patterns. Its central idea is that a garden, though made by people, should seem to have arisen naturally. The book survived in Japan, where it was known as Dakaten, and was rediscovered in China in the 1930s. None of Ji Cheng's own gardens survives.

name: Liang Sicheng
bio: Architect and historian who founded the modern study of Chinese architecture and, with Lin Huiyin, rediscovered the Tang hall of Foguang Temple.
bio_full: Liang Sicheng was the eldest son of the reformer Liang Qichao, born in Tokyo during his father's exile. He studied architecture at the University of Pennsylvania from 1924 to 1927, married the architect and poet Lin Huiyin, and in 1928 founded the architecture department of Northeastern University in Shenyang. From 1931 he led field research at the Society for Research in Chinese Architecture, surveying hundreds of old buildings in difficult conditions, and in 1937 identified the Tang dynasty East Hall of Foguang Temple. After 1946 he founded the architecture department at Tsinghua University.

Liang decoded the Song Yingzao Fashi and the Qing building regulations and wrote the first modern history of Chinese architecture, illustrated with his own measured drawings. After 1949 he helped design the national emblem and the Monument to the People's Heroes, and argued, unsuccessfully, for preserving the walls and gates of old Beijing. He was persecuted during the Cultural Revolution and died in 1972; his reputation and his conservation ideas were restored after his death.

name: Lin Huiyin
bio: Architect, architectural historian and poet who worked with Liang Sicheng on the survey of China's ancient buildings and the designs of the early People's Republic.
bio_full: Lin Huiyin grew up in a scholarly official family and travelled to London with her father as a teenager. She studied at the University of Pennsylvania from 1924, taking a degree in fine arts because the architecture school did not then award degrees to women, though she took its courses, and then studied stage design at Yale. She married Liang Sicheng in 1928 and became his partner in teaching and research, taking part in field surveys across northern China, including the identification of Foguang Temple in 1937. She was also a celebrated modernist poet and writer.

Lin contributed historical essays and much of the analysis in their joint work, and in the 1950s she was a professor at Tsinghua University. She took part in designing the national emblem of the People's Republic and the decorative reliefs and patterns of the Monument to the People's Heroes, and worked to revive the craft of Beijing cloisonné. Long ill with tuberculosis, she died in 1955 at the age of fifty.

name: Lü Yanzhi
bio: Architect who won the competition for the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing and became the pioneer of a modern Chinese national style.
bio_full: Lü Yanzhi studied at Tsinghua and then at Cornell University, graduating in architecture in 1918. He worked in the office of the American architect Henry Murphy, who was adapting Chinese palace forms to modern college buildings, and returned to China to practise in Shanghai. In 1925 he won the competition for the mausoleum of Sun Yat-sen on Purple Mountain outside Nanjing, and in 1926 the competition for the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall in Guangzhou.

His designs used modern construction in reinforced concrete under traditional blue-tiled roofs, and the mausoleum's plan, a long ascending stairway towards a memorial hall, was read as a bell, a symbol of awakening. Lü died of cancer at the age of thirty-five, before either building was complete. His work set the pattern for the official 'Chinese renaissance' style of the Nationalist government.

name: I. M. Pei
bio: Chinese-American architect of geometric modern buildings, whose late works in Hong Kong and Suzhou engaged directly with Chinese tradition.
bio_full: Ieoh Ming Pei grew up in Hong Kong, Shanghai and his family's home city of Suzhou, where he played in the Lion Grove Garden, then owned by his family. He went to the United States in 1935 to study architecture at the University of Pennsylvania and MIT, and later at Harvard under Gropius. He worked for the developer William Zeckendorf before founding his own firm, whose works included the East Building of the National Gallery in Washington and the glass pyramid of the Louvre. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1983.

In China Pei designed the Fragrant Hill Hotel near Beijing (1982) as an attempt at a modern Chinese architecture, then the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong (1990), a soaring triangulated prism, and in his late eighties the Suzhou Museum (2006), a reinterpretation of the white walls, grey roofs and rockeries of the Suzhou garden. His Chinese work shows a lifelong concern with how modern geometry might carry a sense of place.

name: Wang Shu
bio: Chinese architect, Pritzker Prize winner in 2012, who builds with recycled tiles and bricks and the craft of traditional builders.
bio_full: Wang Shu studied architecture in Nanjing and at Tongji University in Shanghai, and in the early 1990s spent years working with craftsmen on building sites rather than designing. In 1997 he founded the Amateur Architecture Studio in Hangzhou with his wife, the architect Lu Wenyu. He heads the school of architecture at the China Academy of Art, whose Xiangshan campus in Hangzhou he designed in the 2000s. In 2012 he became the first Chinese citizen to win the Pritzker Prize.

Wang's work is a response to the demolition of old Chinese towns during the building boom. He reuses millions of salvaged bricks and tiles in a technique derived from the wapan walls of Zhejiang villages, and draws on the composition of Chinese landscape painting and gardens. The Ningbo Museum and the Xiangshan campus are his best-known buildings; with Lu Wenyu he has also worked on the regeneration of villages.

name: Shunjōbō Chōgen
bio: Buddhist monk who led the rebuilding of Tōdai-ji after 1181, introducing the bold Daibutsuyō ('Great Buddha style') from southern China.
bio_full: Chōgen was born into a minor warrior family in Kyoto, became a monk of the Shingon school at Daigo-ji and practised as a wandering ascetic devoted to the Pure Land. By his own account he travelled to Song China several times, and he came back with knowledge of Chinese building and engineering. When Tōdai-ji in Nara was burned by Taira forces in 1180, the court appointed him in 1181, at about sixty, to raise funds and direct the reconstruction, which he did for the rest of his life, working with Chinese craftsmen such as the caster Chen Heqing.

For Tōdai-ji Chōgen used a structural system from Fujian: tall columns tied together by penetrating tie-beams and bracket arms inserted directly into the columns, with exposed rafters and no ceiling. It allowed enormous buildings to be built quickly from smaller timbers. The Great South Gate (Nandaimon) and the Jōdo-dō of Jōdo-ji at Ono are the main surviving examples. A celebrated wooden portrait statue of the aged Chōgen is preserved at Tōdai-ji.

name: Musō Soseki
bio: Rinzai Zen master, adviser to emperors and shōguns, and the most celebrated garden designer of medieval Japan.
bio_full: Musō Soseki was born in Ise Province, studied esoteric Buddhism and then Zen, and spent years in retreat in remote hermitages before being drawn into the service of Emperor Go-Daigo and then of the Ashikaga shōguns. He headed major monasteries in Kyoto and Kamakura and in 1339 became founding abbot of Tenryū-ji, built by Ashikaga Takauji in memory of Go-Daigo. Seven emperors honoured him with the title of National Master. His disciples made the Five Mountains monasteries centres of Chinese learning and literature.

Musō treated garden making as a form of Zen practice and wrote that a garden can be a means to awakening. Gardens associated with him include those of Zuisen-ji in Kamakura, Tenryū-ji and Saihō-ji, the 'Moss Temple', which he restored in 1339 with a pond garden below and a dry stone cascade above. These gardens, combining pond, rock arrangement and borrowed scenery, shaped Japanese garden design for centuries. Some attributions are traditional rather than documented.

name: Sen no Rikyū
bio: Tea master who perfected wabi tea and designed the tiny rustic tea room, of which the Tai-an at Myōki-an is the only surviving example attributed to him.
bio_full: Sen no Rikyū, born Tanaka Yoshirō to a merchant family in the port city of Sakai, studied tea with Takeno Jōō and practised Zen at Daitoku-ji. He became tea master to Oda Nobunaga and then to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, whose great tea gatherings he organised and for whom he served as a political confidant. In 1591, for reasons that are still debated, Hideyoshi ordered him to commit suicide. His descendants founded the Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke schools of tea.

Rikyū shrank the tea room to two tatami mats or less, with walls of rough earth plaster, small paper windows, a low crawl-through entrance (nijiriguchi) and an alcove for a single scroll or flower, so that host and guests met as equals in a dim, quiet space. This aesthetic of poverty and restraint, wabi, transformed Japanese architecture and design. The Tai-an at Myōki-an in Yamazaki, of about 1582, is traditionally attributed to him.
portrait_caption: Painted portrait of Sen no Rikyū

name: Kobori Enshū
bio: Daimyō, tea master and commissioner of works for the Tokugawa, who designed gardens, tea rooms and palace interiors in a refined style known as kirei-sabi.
bio_full: Kobori Masakazu, called Enshū after his court title, was the son of a vassal of Toyotomi Hideyoshi and became a minor daimyō under the Tokugawa. As commissioner of works (sakuji bugyō) he supervised building at imperial palaces, castles such as Fushimi and Nijō, and temples in Kyoto. He studied tea with Furuta Oribe and became tea instructor to the third shōgun, Tokugawa Iemitsu. The Enshū school of tea continues today.

Enshū's style, often described as kirei-sabi or 'elegant rusticity', added brightness, clear geometry and courtly refinement to Rikyū's austerity. Works associated with him include the crane-and-turtle garden of Konchi-in at Nanzen-ji, the Kohō-an sub-temple of Daitoku-ji with its tea room Bōsen, and work on the Ninomaru garden of Nijō Castle. Many other gardens, including Katsura, were later credited to him by tradition, and such attributions are often doubtful.

name: Prince Hachijō Toshihito
bio: Imperial prince and scholar of classical poetry who founded the Katsura villa in Kyoto, enlarged by his son Prince Toshitada.
bio_full: Toshihito was a younger brother of Emperor Go-Yōzei. As a boy he was adopted by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had no heir at the time, but the adoption was dissolved when Hideyoshi's son was born, and he was given a new princely house, the Hachijō-no-miya. He was a leading scholar of the Kokinshū and received its secret teachings, and he devoted himself to poetry, tea and the arts. Around 1615 he began a villa on the Katsura River west of Kyoto, an area associated with the Tale of Genji.

Toshihito built the Old Shoin and the first gardens; his son Prince Toshitada (1619–1662) restored and greatly enlarged the estate from the 1640s, adding the Middle Shoin, the New Palace and tea houses. The design, a stroll garden around a pond with buildings in the sukiya style, is traditionally credited to Kobori Enshū, but it is now generally seen as the work of the princes themselves with their craftsmen.
portrait_caption: Painted portrait of Prince Hachijō Toshihito

name: Nakai Masakiyo
bio: Master carpenter to Tokugawa Ieyasu, who directed the building of the shogunate's castles and palaces in the early seventeenth century.
bio_full: Nakai Masakiyo came from a family of carpenters in Yamato, the province of the great Nara temples. He entered the service of Tokugawa Ieyasu and after the battle of Sekigahara in 1600 became head carpenter (daiku-gashira) of the new shogunate, receiving a court rank and an income of a lord. He directed work on Fushimi Castle, Nijō Castle in Kyoto, Edo Castle, Sunpu Castle and Nagoya Castle, and on major temples, organising the carpenters of the Kyoto region.

The Nakai family remained hereditary heads of the shogunate's carpenters in the Kyoto region throughout the Edo period, and their archive of plans is an important source for the history of Japanese construction. Masakiyo's work at Nijō Castle, with its sequence of audience halls in the shoin style, shows the formal language of Tokugawa power at its height.

name: Kōra Munehiro
bio: Master carpenter of the Tokugawa shogunate who directed the lavish rebuilding of Nikkō Tōshō-gū in 1634–36.
bio_full: Kōra Munehiro came from Kōra in Ōmi Province, a region known for its builders, and entered the service of the Tokugawa, working on Fushimi Castle and then in Edo. He became one of the shogunate's master carpenters and founded a family that held that office for generations. His best-known project was the rebuilding of the shrine-mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu at Nikkō, ordered by the third shōgun Iemitsu.

At Nikkō Munehiro and his workshop produced the most elaborate ensemble of Japanese architecture: gongen-zukuri shrine halls joined by a linking room, covered with lacquer, gold leaf and dense polychrome carving, culminating in the Yōmeimon gate. Later taste often found it excessive, but it marks the apex of Momoyama and early Edo decorative ambition.

name: Josiah Conder
name_native: ジョサイア・コンドル
bio: English architect who taught the first generation of Japanese architects in Meiji Tokyo and designed the Rokumeikan.
bio_full: Josiah Conder trained in London under the Gothic Revival architect William Burges and won the Soane Medallion in 1876. In 1877, aged twenty-four, he was hired by the Meiji government to teach architecture at the Imperial College of Engineering in Tokyo, where his first students included Tatsuno Kingo, Katayama Tōkuma and Sone Tatsuzō. He went on to design government buildings, the Rokumeikan reception hall (1883), the Russian Orthodox Nikolai Cathedral, offices for Mitsubishi and mansions for the Iwasaki family. He stayed in Japan for the rest of his life, married a Japanese wife and died in Tokyo in 1920.

Conder's buildings mixed Gothic, Renaissance and colonial motifs, sometimes with Indo-Saracenic touches meant to evoke 'the East'. More lasting was his teaching, which created the Japanese architectural profession, and his deep interest in Japanese culture: he studied painting with Kawanabe Kyōsai and wrote pioneering English books on Japanese gardens and flower arrangement. A statue of him stands at the University of Tokyo.

name: Tatsuno Kingo
bio: Leading Meiji architect, pupil of Josiah Conder, who designed the Bank of Japan and Tokyo Station.
bio_full: Tatsuno Kingo was born into a low-ranking samurai family of the Karatsu domain and graduated in 1879 at the top of the first architecture class of the Imperial College of Engineering, taught by Josiah Conder. He studied further in London, including in the office of William Burges, and toured Europe. Returning in 1883 he succeeded Conder as professor, helped found the Architectural Institute of Japan and trained a generation of architects. He died in the influenza pandemic of 1919.

Tatsuno's major works are the Bank of Japan head office (1896), a stone building in a Renaissance manner, and Tokyo Station (1914), a long red-brick building banded with white stone and crowned by domes. This 'Tatsuno style', derived from the English Queen Anne manner, was repeated in banks and offices across Japan, Korea and Taiwan. It symbolised Japan's determination to build a modern state on Western lines.

name: Katayama Tōkuma
bio: Architect to the Imperial Household who designed the neo-Baroque Akasaka Palace and the national museums of Nara and Kyoto.
bio_full: Katayama Tōkuma came from the Chōshū domain, whose leaders dominated the Meiji government, and was a member of the first class of Josiah Conder's architecture students, graduating in 1879. He entered the Imperial Household Ministry and spent his career designing for the imperial family, travelling in Europe to study palaces and furnishings.

His works include the Nara Imperial Museum (1894) and the Kyoto Imperial Museum (1895), both in a French Renaissance manner, and above all the Tōgū Palace, now the State Guest House at Akasaka (1909), modelled on European palaces such as Versailles and the Louvre. It is the most ambitious work of Japanese Western-style architecture; the Meiji Emperor reportedly found it too extravagant. It became the first postwar building designated a National Treasure, in 2009.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright
name_native: フランク・ロイド・ライト
bio: American architect whose Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, built 1917–23, was a landmark of modern architecture in Japan.
bio_full: Wright studied briefly at the University of Wisconsin and worked for Louis Sullivan in Chicago before opening his own practice in 1893. He visited Japan in 1905, became a major collector and dealer of Japanese woodblock prints, and acknowledged the influence of Japanese architecture on his open plans and low, sheltering roofs. From 1917 to 1922 he spent long periods in Tokyo designing the new Imperial Hotel, together with smaller works such as the Myōnichikan school building and the Yamamura house in Ashiya. His assistants there included Antonin Raymond and Arata Endō.

The Imperial Hotel, of brick and carved Ōya stone on a floating foundation, opened in 1923 and famously survived the Great Kantō earthquake. Its demolition in 1968 caused protests, and its entrance and lobby were reconstructed at the Meiji Mura museum in Inuyama. Wright's Japanese years left a body of buildings and pupils, and his 'organic architecture' found many admirers among later Japanese architects.

name: Antonin Raymond
name_native: アントニン・レーモンド
bio: Czech-born American architect who came to Tokyo with Frank Lloyd Wright and became a pioneer of modern architecture in Japan.
bio_full: Raymond studied in Prague, emigrated to the United States in 1910 and worked for Cass Gilbert and then Frank Lloyd Wright, with whom he travelled to Tokyo in 1919 to work on the Imperial Hotel. He soon set up his own office in Tokyo and stayed, with interruptions for the war, until 1973. His own house at Reinanzaka (1924) was one of the first modernist houses in exposed reinforced concrete anywhere. Kunio Maekawa and Junzō Yoshimura were among his assistants.

Raymond combined modern concrete construction with lessons from Japanese timber building: frank structure, natural materials, sliding screens and integration with gardens. St Paul's Church in Karuizawa (1935), with its exposed timber frame, and the Gunma Music Center (1961) are among his best-known works. He was an important link between Wright, European modernism and the postwar generation of Japanese architects.

name: Kunio Maekawa
bio: Japanese architect who worked for Le Corbusier and Antonin Raymond and became a founder of postwar Japanese modernism.
bio_full: Maekawa graduated from Tokyo Imperial University in 1928 and left immediately for Paris, where he worked for two years in Le Corbusier's studio. Back in Tokyo he worked for Antonin Raymond before opening his own office in 1935, entering competitions with modernist designs that challenged the official 'imperial crown' style of the 1930s. Kenzō Tange was one of his assistants.

After the war Maekawa built concert halls, libraries and museums in exposed concrete and tile, among them the Kanagawa Prefectural Music Hall and Library (1954), the Tokyo Bunka Kaikan (1961) facing Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art in Ueno, and the Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum (1975). He developed durable fired-tile cladding for concrete and argued for architecture as a public, democratic art.

name: Junzō Sakakura
bio: Japanese architect who worked for Le Corbusier, designed the Japanese pavilion at the 1937 Paris Exposition and the Museum of Modern Art in Kamakura.
bio_full: Sakakura studied art history at Tokyo Imperial University and then went to Paris, where he worked in Le Corbusier's studio from 1931 to 1936. His Japanese pavilion at the Paris International Exposition of 1937, a light steel frame with ramps and glass, won a grand prize. In Japan he founded a large practice and helped bring Charlotte Perriand to Japan in 1940.

His Museum of Modern Art in Kamakura (1951), a white box raised on slender columns over a lotus pond in the precinct of the Tsurugaoka Hachimangū shrine, was the first public modern art museum in Japan and a model of postwar modernism. He later designed the redevelopment of Shinjuku Station's west exit plaza and many public buildings.

name: Kenzō Tange
bio: The leading Japanese architect of the postwar era, designer of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park and the Yoyogi National Gymnasium.
bio_full: Tange grew up partly in Imabari on Shikoku, studied at Tokyo Imperial University and worked for Kunio Maekawa. In 1949 he won the competition for the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, completed in 1955 with its museum raised on pilotis aligned with the ruined Genbaku Dome. As a professor at the University of Tokyo his laboratory trained Fumihiko Maki, Arata Isozaki, Kishō Kurokawa and others. His 1960 Plan for Tokyo, a linear city across Tokyo Bay, inspired the Metabolists. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1987.

Tange's buildings of the 1950s and 1960s, such as the Kagawa Prefectural Office (1958), translated the post-and-beam of Japanese timber building into concrete. His Yoyogi gymnasiums for the 1964 Olympics, hung from cables in great swooping curves, and the stainless-steel St Mary's Cathedral in Tokyo are masterpieces of structural expression. Later his office worked worldwide, and the twin-towered Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (1991) became a symbol of the city.

name: Kiyonori Kikutake
bio: Founding member of the Metabolist group, known for his Sky House and visionary floating Marine City.
bio_full: Kikutake studied at Waseda University and opened his office in Tokyo in 1953. In 1960 he was one of the authors of the Metabolism manifesto presented at the World Design Conference in Tokyo, contributing projects for cities floating on the sea. Toyo Itō was among his assistants.

His own Sky House (1958), a single square room raised on four concrete panels with service units that could be replaced, was a manifesto of Metabolist thinking. He designed the administration building of Izumo Taisha (1963), the floating Aquapolis for the 1975 Okinawa Expo and the Edo-Tokyo Museum (1993), lifted high on four massive legs. He saw architecture as a framework that could change and grow over time.

name: Kishō Kurokawa
bio: Metabolist architect of the Nakagin Capsule Tower and later the National Art Center, Tokyo, and a theorist of 'symbiosis'.
bio_full: Kurokawa studied at Kyoto University and then under Kenzō Tange at the University of Tokyo. At twenty-six he was the youngest member of the Metabolist group in 1960. He became one of the best-known architects in Japan, a media figure and prolific writer, and built extensively abroad, including the Kuala Lumpur International Airport and the Van Gogh Museum extension in Amsterdam.

His Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) put the Metabolist idea of replaceable units into practice, with prefabricated capsules bolted to two concrete cores. Later he developed a philosophy of 'symbiosis' between tradition and technology and between humans and nature, seen in the undulating glass facade of the National Art Center, Tokyo (2007). He ran for governor of Tokyo in the year of his death.

name: Fumihiko Maki
bio: Japanese architect of quietly crafted modernism, associated with Metabolism, and winner of the Pritzker Prize in 1993.
bio_full: Maki studied under Kenzō Tange at the University of Tokyo and then at Cranbrook and Harvard, and taught at Washington University in St. Louis and Harvard. He took part in the Metabolism manifesto of 1960 with an essay on 'group form', the idea that cities grow from collections of related buildings rather than single megastructures. He returned to Tokyo to found his office in 1965.

His Hillside Terrace in Daikanyama, built in phases from 1969 to 1992, is a celebrated example of incremental urban design. Spiral (1985), the Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium (1990) and 4 World Trade Center in New York (2013) show his precise use of metal, glass and layered space. He continued to practise into his nineties and died in 2024.

name: Arata Isozaki
bio: Japanese architect and theorist who moved from Metabolism to a postmodern play of forms, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 2019.
bio_full: Isozaki grew up in Ōita, which was bombed in the war, and studied and worked under Kenzō Tange before opening his own office in 1963. Close to the Metabolists but critical of their optimism, he wrote of the city as ruin. His early works in Ōita, including the Ōita Prefectural Library (1966), were followed by the Gunma Prefectural Museum of Modern Art (1974), built as a framework of cubes.

The Tsukuba Center Building (1983), quoting Michelangelo's Campidoglio and other Western sources, became a landmark of postmodernism, and his Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles (1986) and Palau Sant Jordi in Barcelona brought him international fame. He was a leading intellectual figure who wrote on Japanese concepts of space, such as ma, and mentored younger architects worldwide.

name: Tadao Andō
bio: Self-taught Japanese architect of meditative buildings in smooth concrete and light, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 1995.
bio_full: Andō grew up in Osaka, worked as a truck driver and boxed professionally before teaching himself architecture through books and travel, including visits to the buildings of Le Corbusier. He opened his office in Osaka in 1969. The small Row House in Sumiyoshi (Azuma House, 1976), with a courtyard open to the sky splitting the house in two, made his name.

Andō builds with precisely cast concrete, simple geometry, water and light, aiming at spaces of contemplation that echo the austerity of Zen and the tea house without imitating them. The Church of the Light (1989), the Water Temple on Awaji Island (1991) and the art museums on Naoshima, including the largely underground Chichu Art Museum (2004), are among his works; he has built widely in Europe, America and China.

name: Toyo Itō
bio: Japanese architect of light, fluid buildings such as the Sendai Mediatheque, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 2013.
bio_full: Itō was born in Seoul, then under Japanese rule, and grew up in Nagano. After studying at the University of Tokyo he worked for Kiyonori Kikutake and opened his own office in 1971. Kazuyo Sejima was among his assistants. His early houses, such as White U (1976), and the Tower of Winds in Yokohama (1986) explored lightness, transparency and the ephemeral city.

The Sendai Mediatheque (2001), with floors carried on tree-like tubes of steel lattice, opened a period of structural experiment that continued with the Tama Art University Library (2007), the TOD'S building in Omotesandō and the National Taichung Theater in Taiwan (2016). After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami he led the Home-for-All project of community buildings for survivors.

name: SANAA (Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa)
bio: Tokyo practice of Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa, known for light, transparent buildings, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 2010.
bio_full: Kazuyo Sejima (born 1956) studied at Japan Women's University and worked for Toyo Itō before founding her own office in 1987. Ryue Nishizawa (born 1966) studied at Yokohama National University and joined her; in 1995 they founded SANAA (Sejima and Nishizawa and Associates), while each keeps a separate practice. Sejima directed the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2010, the year the two received the Pritzker Prize.

SANAA's buildings dissolve mass into thin white planes, glass and open, non-hierarchical plans. The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art in Kanazawa (2004), a glass disc containing scattered galleries, the New Museum in New York, the Rolex Learning Center in Lausanne and the Louvre-Lens are among their works. Nishizawa's Teshima Art Museum (2010), a concrete shell open to the sky, made with the artist Rei Naitō, is often counted among the finest recent Japanese buildings.

name: Kengo Kuma
bio: Japanese architect known for buildings of timber slats, bamboo and stone that seek to 'erase' architecture, including the Japan National Stadium.
bio_full: Kuma studied at the University of Tokyo and at Columbia University, and opened his office in Tokyo in 1990. After an early postmodern phase he turned, in the 1990s, to what he called 'anti-object' architecture, in which buildings are broken down into small elements of natural material and dissolve into their surroundings. Commissions for small towns such as Yusuhara in Kōchi helped him develop work with local craftsmen.

His Nezu Museum in Tokyo (2009), with a deep sheltering roof and bamboo-lined approach, the V&A Dundee in Scotland (2018) and the Japan National Stadium (2019), built for the Tokyo Olympics with eaves of Japanese cedar, are among his best-known works. His office has become one of the most prolific in the world.

name: Shigeru Ban
bio: Japanese architect known for structures of paper tubes and for disaster-relief architecture, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 2014.
bio_full: Ban studied at the Southern California Institute of Architecture and Cooper Union in New York, and opened his office in Tokyo in 1985. From the late 1980s he developed structures of recycled cardboard tubes, which are cheap, strong and easily assembled. After the Kobe earthquake of 1995 he built emergency shelters and a paper church for the victims, and he has since built relief housing and community buildings after disasters around the world.

Alongside this humanitarian work Ban designs museums and houses that explore woven timber, paper and movable walls, among them the Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010), the Cardboard Cathedral in Christchurch (2013) and the Ōita Prefectural Art Museum (2015). The Pritzker jury praised his combination of innovation and responsibility.

name: Abiji
bio: Baekje master builder who, according to tradition, raised the nine-storey wooden pagoda of Hwangnyongsa in the Silla capital in 645.
bio_full: Abiji is known only from the thirteenth-century Samguk yusa, which records that Queen Seondeok of Silla, advised by the monk Jajang, invited a master craftsman from the rival kingdom of Baekje to build a great pagoda at the royal temple of Hwangnyongsa in Gyeongju. Abiji led some two hundred workers, and the pagoda was completed in 645.

The pagoda, said to have been about eighty metres tall, had nine storeys symbolising the nine neighbouring peoples whom Silla hoped to overcome. It was struck by lightning and repaired several times and finally burned during the Mongol invasion of 1238. Only its foundation stones remain. Abiji's story illustrates the reputation of Baekje builders, who also built Japan's first temples.

name: Kim Dae-seong
bio: Unified Silla minister traditionally credited with founding Bulguksa and the Seokguram grotto near Gyeongju.
bio_full: Kim Dae-seong was a high official of the Unified Silla kingdom who served as chief minister in the 740s and 750s. The Samguk yusa, written five centuries later, tells the legend that he was reborn into a noble family as a reward for piety in a previous life, and that in 751 he began Bulguksa for his parents in this life and Seokguram for his parents in his former life.

He died in 774 before the works were finished, and the state completed them. How far he directed the design is unknown, and the account is legendary, but the date and the high quality of the two monuments point to court patronage of the highest level. Together they are regarded as the summit of Silla Buddhist architecture and sculpture.

name: Jeong Yak-yong
bio: Joseon Silhak scholar who designed the Hwaseong Fortress at Suwon for King Jeongjo, using cranes and pulleys of his own design.
bio_full: Jeong Yak-yong, known as Dasan, passed the civil service examination in 1789 and became a favourite of King Jeongjo. In 1792 the king commissioned him to plan the walls of the new city of Hwaseong at Suwon, around the tomb of the king's father. Drawing on Chinese and Western books, Jeong designed the fortifications and lifting devices, including the geojunggi crane, that sped up construction between 1794 and 1796. After Jeongjo's death in 1800 he was exiled for eighteen years because of his links with Catholicism.

In exile at Gangjin he wrote some five hundred volumes on government, law, medicine and the classics, most famously the Mongmin simseo on the duties of local officials. Hwaseong combined Korean and Chinese fortification practice with brick construction and new technology, and its detailed building record, the Hwaseong seongyeok uigwe, made its faithful restoration possible after the Korean War.

name: Yi Hwang
bio: The greatest Neo-Confucian philosopher of Joseon Korea, who built the Dosan study hall from which the Dosan Seowon academy grew.
bio_full: Yi Hwang, known as Toegye, passed the civil service examination in 1534 and held a series of offices, but repeatedly withdrew to his home district near Andong to study and teach. In 1561 he completed the Dosan Seodang, a small study hall and teaching building whose design he planned himself, on a site facing the Nakdong River. Disciples gathered there in great numbers.

After his death in 1570 his followers built the Dosan Seowon around the hall in 1574, and the king granted it a royal charter the following year. The modest seodang, with its tiny room, veranda and small pond, expresses Yi Hwang's ideal of a life of quiet self-cultivation, and the academy became the model for Confucian seowon across Korea.

name: Yang San-bo
bio: Joseon scholar who withdrew from public life and created Soswaewon, the most celebrated private garden of Korea.
bio_full: Yang San-bo was a disciple of the reforming Confucian official Jo Gwang-jo. When Jo was purged and executed in 1519, Yang, still a young man, renounced an official career and retired to his home in Damyang, South Jeolla Province, where he built the garden of Soswaewon ('Garden of Clear and Fresh Breeze').

Soswaewon is a small garden along a mountain stream, with pavilions, an earthen wall and bamboo groves, designed to blend with the existing landscape rather than reshape it. It became a gathering place for poets such as Song Sun and Jeong Cheol, and a woodblock print of 1755 records its layout. It is the classic expression of the Korean ideal of a scholar's retreat in nature.

name: Kim Swoo-geun
bio: South Korean architect of the Space Group building and the Seoul Olympic Stadium, a central figure in Korean modern architecture.
bio_full: Kim Swoo-geun was born in the north of Korea under Japanese rule, studied at Seoul National University and then in Tokyo at the Tokyo University of the Arts and the University of Tokyo. Returning to Seoul in 1960 he won major commissions and in 1966 founded the magazine Space, which became the centre of Korean architectural and artistic debate. His Space Group office trained many Korean architects.

Kim's early concrete works showed the influence of Japanese modernism, and his design for the Buyeo National Museum (1967) was criticised for resembling a Japanese shrine. He later developed a language of dark brick, intimate scale and layered space inspired by traditional Korean houses, seen in the Space Group building (1971–77) and the Kyungdong Church (1981). His Olympic Stadium (1984), with curves derived from Joseon porcelain, was built for the 1988 Seoul Olympics.

name: Kim Chung-up
bio: South Korean architect who worked for Le Corbusier and designed the French Embassy in Seoul.
bio_full: Kim Chung-up studied architecture in Yokohama and in 1952 joined the studio of Le Corbusier in Paris, where he worked until 1956 on projects including Chandigarh. Back in Seoul he founded his own office and taught. His criticism of the government's urban policies led to his forced exile in 1971; he lived in France and the United States until 1979.

The French Embassy in Seoul (1962), with its sweeping concrete roofs evoking traditional Korean eaves, is regarded as a landmark of Korean modern architecture. Kim's other works include the Samil Building (1970), once the tallest building in Seoul, and the World Peace Gate at the Olympic Park (1988).

name: Qin and Han imperial builders
bio: The conscript labourers, craftsmen and officials who built the palaces and tombs of the first Chinese empires; this entry gathers works whose designers are unknown.
bio_full: The Qin and Han states built on a colossal scale by mobilising conscripted labour, convicts and specialist craftsmen under ministries of works. Historians such as Sima Qian record the numbers involved, and the names of a few officials and many workshop marks survive on bricks, tiles and figures, but no architect in the modern sense can be identified for their palaces and tombs.

Their buildings of rammed earth and timber rose on high terraces arranged along axes within walled enclosures, a model of imperial planning that lasted two thousand years. Almost everything above ground has vanished, but excavated foundations, pottery models and tombs designed as underground palaces show the beginnings of the Chinese architectural tradition.

name: Builders of the Great Wall
bio: The soldiers, conscripts, convicts and craftsmen of many dynasties who built and rebuilt the frontier walls of northern China.
bio_full: From the Warring States to the Ming, walls along the northern frontier were built by armies and by forced labour drafted from the population, often in harsh conditions; legends such as that of Lady Meng Jiang, whose tears brought down a section of wall where her husband had died, preserve the memory of their suffering. Under the Ming, military officials such as Qi Jiguang directed the construction of brick watchtowers and garrisons.

Over two thousand years their methods changed from tamped earth and reed layers in the western deserts to fired brick and dressed stone near Beijing. The collective result is the largest building project in human history, though it was never a single wall and never completed as a unified plan.

name: Chinese Buddhist cave and pagoda builders
bio: The monks, donors, sculptors and masons who carved China's cave temples and built its brick and stone pagodas; this entry gathers works without a known designer.
bio_full: Buddhist cave temples and pagodas were commissioned by emperors, officials, monks and lay societies, whose names often survive in dedicatory inscriptions, while the stone carvers, painters and masons who made them are rarely recorded. Workshops moved along the Silk Road and between capitals, carrying styles from Central Asia into China.

These builders adapted the Indian rock-cut sanctuary and the stupa to Chinese conditions, creating the multi-storey pagoda in timber, brick and stone and imitating timber forms in stone and brick. Their works preserve the best evidence for early Chinese architecture, since so few early timber buildings survive.

name: Tang dynasty carpenters
bio: The anonymous master carpenters of the Tang dynasty, whose only surviving buildings in China are a few remote temple halls.
bio_full: The great Tang capital of Chang'an and its palaces and monasteries were built by official workshops and guilds of carpenters whose names are almost entirely lost. The persecution of Buddhism in 845 and later wars destroyed nearly all Tang timber buildings, leaving only a handful of halls in the mountains of Shanxi.

Their work is known also from murals, tomb models and, above all, from Japan, where temples such as Tōshōdai-ji were built by craftsmen trained in Tang methods. The Tang system of columns, interlocking bracket sets and deep eaves became the classical language of East Asian timber architecture.

name: Liao and Song builders
bio: The carpenters and masons of the Liao and Song dynasties, whose pagodas and halls are the best-preserved medieval buildings of China.
bio_full: Under the Khitan Liao in the north and the Song in the centre and south, building was organised by official bureaus and local workshops, and donors' names are recorded in inscriptions, but the carpenters who designed the buildings are seldom named. Their practices were codified in the Song Yingzao Fashi of 1103.

Liao builders preserved the robust proportions of Tang architecture, while the Song developed slenderer forms and more elaborate bracketing and decoration. Their surviving works, including the world's tallest timber pagoda and the Iron Pagoda of Kaifeng, were among the first buildings studied by Liang Sicheng and his colleagues in the 1930s.

name: Ming imperial builders
bio: The official designers, craftsmen and labourers who built the palaces, altars and tombs of the Ming court.
bio_full: Ming imperial construction was directed by the Ministry of Works and eunuch-run offices, which mobilised craftsmen from across the empire, many from the Suzhou region, together with soldiers and conscripted labourers. Timber was brought from the forests of the south-west, bricks fired at specified kilns and stamped with makers' names, and stone quarried near Beijing.

A few master craftsmen such as Kuai Xiang are named in records, but most of the designers are anonymous. Their buildings follow strict conventions of rank, colour and number, and they established the form of Beijing that the Qing inherited.

name: Qing imperial builders
bio: The court designers, craftsmen and labourers of the Qing dynasty, who built palaces, gardens and temples across the empire.
bio_full: The Qing court continued the Ming system of imperial construction under the Ministry of Works and the Imperial Household Department, with hereditary design families such as the Lei. In 1734 the court issued its own building regulations, the Gongcheng zuofa zeli, which fixed the dimensions and labour for official buildings.

Qing builders expanded the imperial repertoire to include Tibetan and Mongolian Buddhist architecture, European-style pavilions designed by Jesuits and vast garden palaces. Their work at Chengde and Beijing reflects the multi-ethnic character of the empire.

name: Tibetan builders
bio: The masons, carpenters and artists of Tibet, who developed a distinct architecture of massive battered walls and flat roofs.
bio_full: Tibetan architecture grew from its own traditions and from Indian and Nepalese Buddhist models rather than from Chinese timber building. Palaces, monasteries and fortresses were built by local masons and carpenters, often with corvée labour, under the direction of lamas and officials; Newar craftsmen from Nepal contributed metalwork and painting.

Its buildings rise from stone and rammed-earth walls that slope inward, with small windows framed in black, painted timber interiors and gilded roofs. The Potala Palace is its supreme monument, and Qing emperors copied it at Chengde.

name: Suzhou garden makers
bio: The owners, painters, rockery masters and craftsmen who created the classical gardens of Suzhou and the lower Yangzi region.
bio_full: Chinese scholar gardens were usually made by their owners, retired officials, merchants and scholars, in collaboration with painters and with specialist rockery masters such as Zhang Nanyang, Zhang Lian and Ge Yuliang, whose names are recorded in literature. The work of the craftsmen is anonymous. Gardens changed hands often and were remade by each owner, so that most of what survives dates from the nineteenth century.

These makers composed gardens as sequences of framed views, drawing on landscape painting and poetry. Their principles were written down by Ji Cheng in the Yuanye and by other late Ming authors. The gardens of Suzhou were inscribed together on the World Heritage List in 1997 and 2000.

name: Vernacular builders of China, Japan and Korea
bio: The farmers, clans and village carpenters who built the houses of East Asia's countryside; this entry gathers vernacular works without known designers.
bio_full: Vernacular houses were built by families and communities with local carpenters and masons, following inherited practice rather than drawings. Their forms responded to climate, materials, family structure and security: earthen walls in Fujian, steep thatch in the snowy Japanese Alps, heated ondol floors and separate quarters in Korean gentry houses.

Long overlooked by historians, these buildings were studied from the twentieth century onward as expressions of everyday life, and several villages have been inscribed as World Heritage Sites. Communal maintenance, such as the rethatching of roofs in Shirakawa-gō, keeps some of them alive.

name: Shinto shrine carpenters
bio: The shrine carpenters (miya-daiku) and priestly communities who have built and periodically rebuilt Japan's Shinto shrines.
bio_full: The great shrines of Japan were built by carpenters attached to shrine and court, and their designs were preserved less in drawings than in the practice of periodic rebuilding. At Ise, every twenty years, the carpenters build new sanctuaries in the same form beside the old, a cycle that takes years of preparation, from cutting cypress trees to the transfer of the deity.

These rebuildings transmit the skills and the ancient forms of Japanese architecture from one generation to the next. Their work raises the question, often debated by modern architects and conservators, of whether authenticity lies in old material or in a continuously renewed form.

name: Asuka and Nara temple builders
bio: The Korean, Chinese and Japanese craftsmen who built Japan's first Buddhist temples; this entry gathers works without known designers.
bio_full: According to the Nihon Shoki, in 588 the Korean kingdom of Baekje sent temple carpenters, a roof-tile maker, a metalworker and a painter to build Asuka-dera, Japan's first full Buddhist temple. Their descendants and Japanese apprentices, organised later in the government's Office for the Construction of Tōdai-ji and similar bodies, built the temples of Asuka and Nara.

These builders introduced to Japan the timber frame with bracket sets, tiled roofs and stone platforms, the temple compound with its pagoda and halls, and the grid capital. Their works at Hōryū-ji, Yakushi-ji, Tōdai-ji and Tōshōdai-ji include the oldest timber buildings in the world.

name: Heian court builders
bio: The carpenters and craftsmen who built the palaces and Pure Land temples of the Heian aristocracy.
bio_full: In the Heian period the court and great families such as the Fujiwara commissioned mansions and temples from carpenters and craftsmen in Kyoto, some of them attached to the government, others in workshops patronised by aristocrats. Patrons such as Fujiwara no Yorimichi are known by name, while the builders are not.

They developed a more Japanese architecture, with cypress-bark roofs, raised wooden floors, pond gardens and halls designed to be seen across water, and created the Amida halls of Pure Land Buddhism. Their palaces are all lost, but are known from picture scrolls such as the Genji Monogatari Emaki.

name: Muromachi Zen temple builders
bio: The carpenters, monks and garden workers who built Japan's Zen monasteries and gardens; this entry gathers works without firmly known designers.
bio_full: Zen monasteries in Kamakura and Kyoto were founded by shōguns and warriors and planned by monks, some of them Chinese, following the monastic layout of Song China. Their gardens were made by monks and by specialist gardeners, including the low-status kawaramono ('riverbank people') such as Zen'ami, who worked for the Ashikaga shōguns.

They introduced the Chinese 'Zen style' of architecture and developed the dry landscape garden, the shoin room and the pavilions of the Kitayama and Higashiyama villas. Many famous gardens have traditional attributions, for instance to Sōami, that cannot be confirmed.

name: Japanese castle builders
bio: The daimyō, master carpenters and stonemasons who built the castles of the age of unification.
bio_full: Castles were commissioned by warlords and planned by them and their retainers, with the stone bases built by specialist masons such as the Anō guild of Ōmi, and the timber keeps raised by master carpenters. Construction of a large castle mobilised thousands of workers under the direction of the daimyō.

Their castles combined defence against firearms with display of power, crowning high stone walls with multi-storeyed white or black keeps. In 1615 the Tokugawa limited each domain to one castle, and after 1873 most were demolished; only twelve original keeps survive.

name: Builders of the Three Kingdoms of Korea
bio: The builders and craftsmen of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, whose temples and tombs are known mainly from stone remains.
bio_full: The three Korean kingdoms adopted Buddhism from the fourth century and built royal tombs, palaces and great temples, with craftsmen trained in Chinese methods and developing distinctive local styles. Baekje builders were so renowned that they were sent to Japan and to Silla to build temples, and a single name, Abiji, survives in the historical record.

Because their timber buildings were all destroyed, their work is known from stone pagodas, foundations, tiles and the murals of Goguryeo tombs. Through Japan's first temples, built by Baekje craftsmen, their influence extended across East Asia.

name: Silla builders
bio: The anonymous builders and craftsmen of the Silla kingdom at Gyeongju.
bio_full: After unifying most of the Korean peninsula in 668, Silla made its capital Gyeongju a city of palaces, temples, tombs and gardens. Royal patrons and ministers are known by name, but the builders of its works are not.

Their surviving works, in stone and earth, show precise geometry and refined proportions: the observatory tower of Cheomseongdae, the pond garden of Wolji and the masonry of Bulguksa and Seokguram. The Gyeongju Historic Areas were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

name: Goryeo and Joseon temple carpenters
bio: The carpenters of Korea's mountain monasteries, who built the oldest surviving timber halls in Korea.
bio_full: Korean Buddhist temples were built and repaired by monk-carpenters and lay craftsmen, often over centuries, and their names appear only occasionally in inscriptions found on roof beams during repairs. Temples in remote mountains survived wars better than those in the cities, so they preserve the oldest timber buildings of the country.

Their halls of the Goryeo period, with column-head bracketing and gently swelling columns, are notable for restraint and proportion, and their storage halls at Haeinsa show remarkable practical knowledge of climate. Seven mountain monasteries were inscribed together as a World Heritage Site in 2018.

name: Joseon royal builders
bio: The officials and craftsmen who built the palaces, shrines and walls of the Joseon capital Seoul.
bio_full: The Joseon court organised construction through government offices that recorded each project in illustrated reports called uigwe, which list materials, costs and the names of craftsmen. The overall plans of the capital were set by scholar-officials such as Jeong Do-jeon, following Confucian ritual texts and geomancy.

Their palaces and shrines are restrained, carefully fitted to the terrain and decorated with painted dancheong patterns. Most were rebuilt after the Japanese invasions of the 1590s, and many again in the nineteenth century and after the damage of colonial rule and war, often with the help of the uigwe records.
